newsitem.title: HONG KONG: H.K. economy seen speeding into fourth quarter.
newsitem.headline: H.K. economy seen speeding into fourth quarter.

text.p: Hong Kong's economy is picking up as it heads into the year's fourth quarter and should be able to meet the government's forecast of 4.7 percent growth for full-year 1996, economists said on Friday.
Improved retail sales, booming stock prices and a reviving property market all pointed to a recovery from the sluggishness that had dogged the economy since late last year, they said.
"The consumption market has improved, more people are shopping over the weekend, and the stock and property markets healthy," said K.K. Chan of the Nomura Research Institute.
The government said on Friday it was keeping its full-year gross domestic product (GDP) growth forecast at 4.7 percent.
The government also said GDP grew at a tentative estimate of 5.0 to 5.5 percent in the third quarter of 1996, against 4.3 percent in the second quarter and 3.3 percent in the first.

"I think it's a very good result for the Hong Kong economy as it heads into the final stages of transition to Chinese sovereignty (next year)," said Ian Perkin, chief economist at the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce.

Meeting the 4.7 percent target requires a further increase of the growth rate in the year's fourth quarter, but economists said that was possible both because fundamentals were improving and because it would be calculated from a relatively low base.

"First we had a very weak fourth quarter last year," Nomura's Chan pointed out. "Last year Q4 was the lowest growth quarter, 3.5 percent growth in 1995 contrasted with 6.1 percent in first quarter of last year."
"And this year, 1996 Q1 we had 3.3 percent growth, it's logical that we may see six percent in Q4."
But some economist warned that the very low numbers recorded in the year's first half still meant reaching the 4.7 percent target was not yet a certainty.
The government also cut its inflation forecast to 6.0 percent from 6.8, further heartening economists.

"Lower inflation means that people throughout the economy are not being affected by the price rises (as) they once were, and also it maintains the competitiveness of Hong Kong in the regional and global scene," the Chamber's Perkin said.
